analysis.one_liner: Ends tax deductions for oil spill cleanup and liability costs.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee on the day it was introduced and never received any further action, dying without a vote despite 29 cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have changed the tax code so that oil companies and shippers could no longer deduct the cost of cleaning up a spill, or the damages they owe for one, from their federal taxes. It covered oil transported by vessel onto waters protected by the Clean Water Act, with exceptions for spills caused solely by acts of God, war, U.S. government negligence, or a third party. It would have applied to tax years starting after December 31, 1988.
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers, who currently share the bill for oil spill cleanup and damages through the tax code because companies write those costs off; coastal communities and fishermen, because a company that cannot deduct spill costs faces a genuinely higher price for spilling; and the Treasury, which would collect more tax from companies that cause spills.

how_it_helps.text: Ends the taxpayer subsidy for oil spills: companies could no longer deduct removal costs — cleanup and damage-mitigation spending — or liability costs — damages owed and the cost of determining them — from their business income.

Applies to oil being transported by or for the taxpayer in a vessel and spilled into waters subject to the Clean Water Act, covering crude oil and any other petroleum product, so it reaches the tanker and shipping side of the industry rather than just refineries.

Includes exceptions so the penalty does not fall on a company for a spill it could not prevent: spills caused solely by an act of God, an act of war, U.S. government negligence, or a third party's act or omission are excluded.
Applies to taxable years beginning after December 31, 1988, meaning costs from spills during 1989 — the year of the Exxon Valdez disaster — would have been covered.

analysis.who_pays: Oil tanker operators, shippers, and anyone transporting crude oil or petroleum products by vessel, who would pay spill cleanup and liability costs out of after-tax dollars instead of deductible ones; some of that added cost would likely flow through to consumers in fuel and shipping prices.

drawbacks.text: Higher after-tax spill costs are a cost of doing business, and some of it would be passed on to consumers through higher prices for fuel and shipped goods.

The bill applied retroactively to amounts paid or incurred in taxable years beginning after December 31, 1988, which means it would have changed the tax treatment of costs companies had already started incurring in 1989 — a retroactive tax increase that businesses could fairly object to.

The carve-outs depend on proving a discharge was caused 'solely' by an excluded cause, which invites litigation over causation — for example, disputes over whether a third party's act was the sole cause of a spill.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real but narrow: it ends a provision of the tax code that lets the companies responsible for a spill deduct the cleanup and damages from their taxes, shifting part of the cost back to taxpayers. The costs — somewhat higher shipping and fuel prices, plus a retroactive effective date and room for causation disputes — are modest by comparison. It is a fairly drawn penalty bill, not a comprehensive oil spill regime; the Exxon Valdez-era liability legislation that passed that year addressed damages and cleanup authority more directly. The main flaw is that it never got serious attention: it sat in committee for the rest of the Congress and was never refined, marked up, or debated.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never acted on it, and it died when the 101st Congress ended in January 1991.

narrative.text: Rep. Louise Slaughter of New York introduced the bill on April 18, 1989, joined by Reps. Peter DeFazio and Jim Jontz as original sponsors — less than a month after the Exxon Valdez tanker spill in Alaska.
The same day, the bill was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means, the committee with jurisdiction over tax law.
Twenty-nine House members cosponsored it — 28 of 257 House Democrats and 1 of 175 House Republicans — but no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever took place.
No further action was ever recorded; the bill remained in committee until the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991, and it never became law.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil tanker operators and petroleum shippers, who kept the ability to deduct spill cleanup and liability costs from their taxes — leaving taxpayers to continue sharing the bill for spills through forgone revenue.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Oil shippers who kept the deduction

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever held; support was modest and heavily Democratic — 28 of 29 cosponsors were Democrats, with one Republican — and the bill died in committee without opposition ever having to go on record.

industries.industry: Oil tanker operators and petroleum shippers
industries.note: Under current law, a company that spills oil can deduct cleanup costs and damage payments as ordinary business expenses, so taxpayers effectively absorb part of every spill bill through forgone tax revenue. This bill would have made those costs nondeductible, raising the after-tax price of a spill — which is exactly why the industry benefited from the bill dying in committee.

industries.industry: Crude oil producers and petroleum traders
industries.note: The bill covers oil 'transported by or for the taxpayer,' so producers and traders who charter tankers or otherwise arrange shipments would also have lost the deduction for spill removal and liability costs, not just the shipping companies themselves.
